I am 68 years old and have been farming these fields in Quzhou County since I was a teenager. Over the decades, I have learned what this land can do. The North China Plain gives us two crops a year if you work it right: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is the system my father used, and it is the system I trust. I have about 12 mu of good irrigated land, and I will plant all of it to this double-cropping rotation again this year.

For the winter wheat, I will rotary till the soil after the autumn harvest to prepare a fine seedbed. I will sow *Jimai 22*, an improved variety that has done well here—good resistance and stable yield. I will put down compound fertilizer as a basal dressing and topdress with urea at the jointing stage. Wheat needs water, so I will irrigate four times: once before winter to help it survive the cold, once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at flowering. I will spray herbicide and insecticide two or three times to keep weeds and aphids under control. I expect about 1,100 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, there is no time to waste. I will plant *Denghai 605*, a hybrid maize, directly into the wheat stubble without tillage. No-tillage saves time, keeps moisture in the soil, and everyone around here does it for maize. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat because the wheat residue returns some nutrients, so I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing and a side-dressing of urea at the big-flare stage. Two irrigations should be enough—one at jointing and one at tasseling. A couple of pesticide sprays for corn borers and weeds will do. With this hybrid, I expect around 1,150 kg per mu.

I thought about cotton, but at my age I do not have the energy for all the hand-picking and the fifteen sprays it seems to need. Wheat and maize are mechanized from sowing to harvest, which is what my back needs now.
